Let

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(2^{-\lfloor 101k/1\rfloor}+2^{-\lfloor 101k/2\rfloor}+\cdots+2^{-\lfloor 101k/100\rfloor}\right).
\]

We will use the fact that \(101\) is an odd prime. In fact, the same argument works for any odd prime \(p\).

For a fixed denominator \(n\), write every positive integer \(k\) uniquely as

\[
k=qn+i,\qquad q\ge 0,\quad 1\le i\le n.
\]

Then

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{pk}{n}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor \frac{p(qn+i)}{n}\right\rfloor
=pq+\left\lfloor \frac{pi}{n}\right\rfloor.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-\lfloor pk/n\rfloor}
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{q=0}^{\infty}
2^{-pq-\lfloor pi/n\rfloor}
=\frac{1}{1-2^{-p}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{-\lfloor pi/n\rfloor}.
\]

Thus

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{p-1}2^{-\lfloor pk/n\rfloor}
=
\frac{1}{2^p-1}
\sum_{n=1}^{p-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{p-\lfloor pi/n\rfloor}.
\]

For \(p=101\), we need to compute

\[
A=\sum_{n=1}^{100}\sum_{i=1}^{n}2^{101-\lfloor 101i/n\rfloor}.
\]

Now let \(c_m\) be the number of pairs \((i,n)\) with \(1\le i\le n\le p-1\) such that

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{pi}{n}\right\rfloor=m.
\]

Then

\[
A=\sum_{m=1}^{p}c_m2^{p-m}.
\]

We determine the \(c_m\).

- If \(i=n\), then \(\lfloor pi/n\rfloor=p\), so \(c_p=p-1\).
- We claim that for \(1\le m\le p-2\),

\[
c_m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]

Also \(c_{p-1}=0\).

To prove the claim, fix \(m\in\{1,\dots,p-2\}\) and set \(a=p-m\), so \(2\le a\le p-1\). For a fixed \(n\), consider the least positive residue \(R(n)\) of \(an\) modulo \(p\). Write

\[
an=pt+R(n),\qquad 1\le R(n)\le p-1.
\]

There is an \(i<n\) with \(\lfloor pi/n\rfloor=m\) if and only if \(R(n)<n\). Indeed, if such an \(i\) exists, then writing \(u=pi-mn\) gives \(1\le u<n\), and

\[
an=pn-mn=p(n-i)+u,
\]

so \(u=R(n)\) and hence \(R(n)<n\). Conversely, if \(R(n)<n\), then \(t=(an-R(n))/p\) satisfies \(1\le t<n\), and setting \(i=n-t\) gives

\[
pi=mn+R(n),
\]

with \(0<R(n)<n\), so \(\lfloor pi/n\rfloor=m\).

It remains to count how many \(n\in\{1,\dots,p-1\}\) satisfy \(R(n)<n\). Since \(a\ne1\), we never have \(R(n)=n\). Also,

\[
R(p-n)\equiv -an\equiv p-R(n)\pmod p,
\]

so

\[
R(p-n)=p-R(n).
\]

Thus \(R(n)<n\) if and only if \(R(p-n)>p-n\). The involution \(n\mapsto p-n\) has no fixed points because \(p\) is odd, so it bijects the set \(\{n:R(n)<n\}\) with the set \(\{n:R(n)>n\}\). These two sets partition \(\{1,\dots,p-1\}\), hence each has size \((p-1)/2\). Therefore

\[
c_m=\frac{p-1}{2}\qquad (1\le m\le p-2).
\]

For \(m=p-1\), we would have \(a=1\), so \(R(n)=n\), and no \(i<n\) works; hence \(c_{p-1}=0\).

Therefore

\[
A
=
c_p+\sum_{m=1}^{p-2}c_m2^{p-m}
=
(p-1)+\frac{p-1}{2}\sum_{m=1}^{p-2}2^{p-m}.
\]

Now

\[
\sum_{m=1}^{p-2}2^{p-m}
=
2^{p-1}+2^{p-2}+\cdots+2^2
=
2^p-4.
\]

Thus

\[
A
=
(p-1)+\frac{p-1}{2}(2^p-4)
=
(p-1)(2^{p-1}-1).
\]

So for an odd prime \(p\),

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{p-1}2^{-\lfloor pk/n\rfloor}
=
\frac{(p-1)(2^{p-1}-1)}{2^p-1}.
\]

Taking \(p=101\), the required sum is

\[
\boxed{\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}}.
\]
